headline: THE JOB WAS LOST AT THE KITCHEN TABLE
hook: The homeowner signs at the kitchen table with the coffee still warm: one page, a total at the bottom, nothing about when the money moves. Weeks later, when the balance stalls, that page is all the crew has, and it doesn't say a word about when they get paid.
angle: Blaming the client for a stalled final payment skips the owner's part: a quote signed with a total and no payment schedule hands the client control of when the money moves.

headline: THE LAST POST IS SET AND HE STOPPED ANSWERING
hook: The last post is plumb, the gate swings clean, and the homeowner who used to text you every morning has gone quiet. You did the job, he's got the fence, and you're the one sitting in the truck chasing him.
angle: An owner's pull on the money shrinks with every finished phase, so by the time the last post is set, the payment terms have already decided whether the balance is a formality or a fight.

headline: 17 MILLION VIEWS ON A TEARDOWN NOBODY SHOULD NEED
hook: On September 13, 2026, a Joliet, Illinois fence crew posted video of themselves tearing out a fence they had installed, after the homeowner allegedly refused to pay, and news coverage put the original past 17 million views. That is a lot of people watching the last resort, and very few asking how the job got there.
angle: The teardown went viral because every owner knows the feeling, but the lesson isn't about the crowbar; the only point where a crew holds real control of the money is the day the payment terms get signed.

headline: THE $1,000 RULE EVERY CREW SHOULD STEAL
hook: In Illinois, the state attorney general says home repair or remodeling work over $1,000 needs a signed written contract before it starts. That's the law in one state. It belongs in every truck in every state, because when the last payment stalls, the first thing anyone asks to see is the contract.
angle: A rule written to protect homeowners is the best collections habit a crew can adopt: put every job over $1,000 in writing with a payment schedule, whether your state makes you or not.

headline: THE FINAL PAYMENT IS DECIDED BEFORE THE FIRST HOLE
hook: Collections feels like a back-office chore that starts when an invoice goes past due. It doesn't. It starts at signing, when the payment schedule either ties the money to finished phases or leaves the timing up to the client.
angle: Collections isn't something you do at the end of a job; the final payment is settled by the schedule written before the first hole is dug, and chasing it later is the price of skipping that step.

headline: A BIGGER DEPOSIT WON'T GET YOU PAID
hook: After a client stiffs you, the gut says take half up front next time. In California, the state licensing board caps down payments on home improvement jobs, and progress payments can't get ahead of the work done and the materials delivered, which tells you where the protection really lives.
angle: A bigger deposit is the wrong fix for a stiffed balance; payments tied to each finished phase, so the work never outruns the money, protect the crew better and still hold up where deposits are capped.

headline: WOULD YOU TEAR OUT A FENCE TO GET PAID?
hook: On September 13, 2026, a fence crew in Joliet, Illinois posted video of themselves tearing out a fence they had installed after the homeowner allegedly refused to pay. The comments turned into a fight over justice versus a lawsuit, and that's the wrong fight: the one worth having happens at the kitchen table, before the first post goes in.
angle: Whether the teardown was right doesn't matter to your business; if the only move left when a client won't pay is a crowbar, the job was lost when the contract was signed without a payment schedule.

headline: WHAT DOES YOUR CONTRACT SAY ABOUT THE LAST PAYMENT?
hook: Pull out the last contract you signed and find the line that says when the final payment is due and what has to be finished to trigger it. If all it gives you is a total, the client decides when you get paid.
angle: "Balance due on completion" is an argument waiting to happen because nobody defined complete; every payment, the last one included, belongs tied to a named phase of work both sides signed.

headline: YOU'RE EITHER PAID BY THE PHASE OR CHASING THE BALANCE
hook: There are two ways a backyard job ends. The client pays for each phase as it's finished and nothing big is riding on the last day, or the crew hands over the whole thing and spends weeks texting about the balance.
angle: Any schedule that lets finished work run ahead of the money turns the owner into a debt collector; phase-tied payments are the structure that keeps the crew in control right up to the last post.

headline: YOU'RE EITHER WRITING CHANGE ORDERS OR GIVING WORK AWAY
hook: The homeowner walks out mid-build and asks if the gate can go a little wider while you're there. You say sure, nobody writes it down, and when the invoice lands higher than the quote, that one word is the whole argument.
angle: Unsigned extras aren't goodwill, they're the seed of the balance dispute; no change gets built without a signed change order, and the clients you like most are the ones who need it most.

headline: FINISHED WORK DESERVES A FINISHED PAYMENT
hook: Every post set plumb and every board run straight is a promise kept by a crew that showed up before sunrise. A written payment schedule is how the client keeps theirs.
angle: Spelling out when you get paid isn't pushy or corporate; it's the same pride that goes into the work, and owners who treat asking in writing as rude pay for that politeness at the end of the job.

headline: NO CREW SHOULD HAVE TO BEG FOR EARNED MONEY
hook: Nobody got into the trades to be a debt collector. You show up in the dark, you build it right, and the money you earned should move without a single begging text.
angle: Chasing money already earned shouldn't be accepted as part of the trade; a crew that sets when it gets paid in writing before the work starts stops asking for its own money like it's a favor.
